The question of whether brain training improves cognitive function is genuinely contested in the scientific literature. On one side, a 2014 review of 31 studies cited by Harvard Health found that engaging in new, challenging activities such as learning an instrument or a new language "improved several aspects of memory like recalling instructions and processing speed" in older adults [d4], and the NIA notes that the ACTIVE trial showed cognitive training benefits persisting for two years in research settings [d1]. St. Luke's Health also reports that "recent studies have shown an improvement in different cognitive domains after completing extended periods of mental training," attributing this to neuroplasticity [d5].

On the other side, a large six-week study with 11,430 participants published in a peer-reviewed journal found that "no evidence was found for transfer effects to untrained tasks, even when those tasks were cognitively closely related," undermining claims of general cognitive improvement from commercial brain training [d3]. A University of Pennsylvania study published in the Journal of Neuroscience found that commercial brain training with Lumosity "had no effect on cognitive function beyond practice effects on the training tasks" [d9][d10]. A 2020 Cochrane meta-analysis of eight clinical trials similarly found only "small, short-term cognitive benefits" with "not enough high-quality research to support the use of brain games for preventing dementia or improving long-term cognitive function" [d7]. Meta-analytic reviews reviewed in ScienceDirect further conclude that "those studies including large samples and active control groups often report no training-related effects," finding that cognitive training programs "do not enhance GCA or any cognitive skill" [d11]. A scientific consensus statement cited in Psychology Today likewise concludes that "the scientific literature does not support claims that the use of software-based 'brain games' alters neural functioning in ways that improve general cognitive performance in everyday life" [d6]. Overall, while some real-world cognitive engagement may offer modest benefits, the evidence strongly conflicts on whether commercial brain-training programs produce meaningful, transferable improvements in general cognitive function [d1][d8].
